title: Floyd-Warshall: all-pairs shortest paths
overview: This module moves from single-source shortest paths (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) to **all-pairs** shortest paths with Floyd-Warshall. You keep one n x n matrix and let every node, one by one, act as a stop-over. The same matrix also tells you whether a negative cycle exists. The practice day repeats Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall on judge problems.

concepts.term: Adjacency matrix as a distance table
concepts.explain: `adj_mat[i][j]` holds the best known cost from `i` to `j`. Start with 0 on the diagonal, the edge weight where an edge exists, and infinity everywhere else.

concepts.term: Relax through a middle node k
concepts.explain: For each pair (i, j) ask: is going i -> k -> j cheaper than what I have? If yes, overwrite. The outer loop **must** be `k`, so that after round k every path may use nodes 0..k as stop-overs.
concepts.snippet:
for k: for i: for j:
  if (d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]) d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j];

concepts.explain: `INT_MAX + something` overflows and becomes a huge negative number. Always check that both halves are not infinity before adding.
After the three loops, if any `d[i][i]` is below 0, node `i` sits on a cycle whose total weight is negative, so shortest paths are not defined.
Relax every edge V-1 times. One extra pass that still improves something means a negative cycle is reachable from the source.
Dijkstra: one source, no negative edges, O(E log V). Bellman-Ford: one source, negative edges allowed, O(V·E). Floyd-Warshall: every pair, small n (about n <= 500), O(n^3).

files.title: Floyd-Warshall on a directed graph
files.what: Reads a weighted directed graph into a matrix, runs the triple loop, and prints the shortest distance between every pair (INF when unreachable).
steps: Read `n` nodes and `e` edges; build `adj_mat[n][n]` with 0 on the diagonal and `INT_MAX` elsewhere.
For each edge `a b c` store `adj_mat[a][b] = c` (only one direction, the graph is directed).
Outer loop `k` picks the stop-over node; inner loops `i`, `j` try every pair.
If both `adj_mat[i][k]` and `adj_mat[k][j]` are finite and their sum is smaller, update `adj_mat[i][j]`.
Print the matrix row by row, writing `INF` for `INT_MAX`.
files.input_note: n e, then e lines `from to weight`. Nodes are 0-based.
files.output_note: Row i, column j is the cheapest cost from i to j. Row 0 is `0 3 4 6`: the direct edge 0->2 costs 7, but 0->1->2 costs 3+1 = 4, so the table keeps 4. Row 1 starts with 9 because 1->2->3->0 = 1+2+6.
files.watch_out: `INT_MAX` comes from `<climits>`; the file does not include it and only compiles because this compiler pulls it in through another header. Add `#include <climits>` to be safe.

check.q: Why must `k` be the outermost loop?
check.a: Because after finishing round k, every pair already knows the best path that uses only nodes 0..k in the middle. If k were inside, a pair could be finalised before the stop-over nodes it needs were processed.

files.title: Detect a negative cycle with Floyd-Warshall
files.what: Same triple loop as before, then checks the diagonal. A negative `adj_mat[i][i]` means a negative cycle, otherwise the full distance table is printed.
steps: Build the matrix and run Floyd-Warshall exactly as in `floyd-warshall.cpp`.
Set `cycle = false`, then look at every `adj_mat[i][i]`.
The diagonal starts at 0. It can only drop below 0 if some path leaves `i` and comes back with a total cost below zero.
If `cycle` is true print the warning, otherwise print the matrix.
files.output_note: The program prints `Negative weighted cycle detected` because going round the cycle makes `adj_mat[0][0]` negative. Remove the edge `2 0 -1` and you get a normal table instead.

check.q: Graph 0->1 (4), 1->0 (-4). Is there a negative cycle?
check.a: No. The cycle costs 4 + (-4) = 0, so the diagonal stays 0, not below 0.

files.title: GfG: Distance from the source (Bellman-Ford)
files.what: The judge's `bellmanFord` function: returns the distance of every node from `src`, 10^8 for unreachable nodes, or `{-1}` if a negative cycle is reachable.
steps: Create `dist(V, 100000000)` (the judge's 'infinity') and set `dist[src] = 0`.
Repeat `V-1` times: for every edge `u v w`, if `dist[u]` is finite and `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]`.
Why V-1? A shortest path without cycles has at most V-1 edges, and each pass fixes at least one more edge of it.
Do one more pass over all edges. If anything still improves, return `{-1}`.
Otherwise return `dist`.
files.input_note: V E, then E edges `u v w`, then the source. This is the judge's second example.
files.output_note: Prints `dist = 1 6 0`, matching the judge's expected `[1, 6, 0]`: from 2 the edge to 0 costs 1, and 2->0->1 costs 1+5 = 6. If a negative cycle were reachable you would see `dist = -1`.
files.watch_out: The file only holds the judge's `Solution` class; the page adds a small test driver to run it.

check.a: An unreachable `u` has no real distance. Adding a negative `w` to the 'infinity' value would wrongly make `v` look reachable.

files.title: GfG: Implementing Floyd-Warshall
files.what: The matrix uses -1 for 'no edge'. The solution turns -1 into infinity, runs Floyd-Warshall in place, then turns infinity back into -1.
steps: Replace every `-1` with `INT_MAX` so the comparisons work (otherwise -1 would look like a very cheap edge).
Run the usual `k`, `i`, `j` loops with the infinity guard.
Replace every remaining `INT_MAX` with `-1` to match the judge's format.
The driver `main` reads `tc` test cases, calls `shortestDistance`, and prints each matrix followed by `~`.
files.complexity: Time O(n^3) per test · Space O(1) extra
files.input_note: Number of tests; for each: n, then the n x n matrix.
files.output_note: First test: `0 1 43` becomes `0 1 7` because 0->1->2 costs 1+6. Row 2 stays `-1 -1 0` since node 2 has no outgoing edges. Each matrix ends with a `~` line.
files.watch_out: The 'convert sentinel, compute, convert back' pattern matters: forgetting the first step makes -1 act like a negative edge.

check.q: What goes wrong if you skip turning -1 into infinity?
check.a: The algorithm treats -1 as an edge of weight -1, so it happily routes through 'missing' edges and produces wrong, too-small distances.

files.title: CSES Shortest Routes II (Floyd-Warshall with queries)
files.what: Undirected graph with possibly repeated roads. Run Floyd-Warshall once with `long long` distances, then answer each query `s d` in O(1), printing -1 when unreachable.
steps: Fill the matrix for nodes 1..n: 0 on the diagonal, `LLONG_MAX` elsewhere.
For every road keep the cheapest one: `adj_mat[a][b] = min(adj_mat[a][b], c)` and the same for `[b][a]`.
Run the triple loop once; this is the expensive O(n^3) part.
For each query just look up `adj_mat[s][d]`; print -1 if it is still `LLONG_MAX`.
files.input_note: n m q, m roads `a b c`, then q queries `s d`. Nodes are 1-based.
files.output_note: The program crashes (access violation) before printing anything. Once fixed it would print 7, 7 and -1 (1->2->3 beats the direct road of 10; node 4 has no roads).
files.watch_out: The matrix is declared `long long adj_mat[n][n]` but the loops use indices 1..n, so index n is outside the array and the program crashes. Fix: declare `adj_mat[n+1][n+1]` (or a global `[505][505]`). Also, a 500x500 local `long long` array is 2 MB; making it global is safer.

check.q: Why read all roads with `min(...)` instead of plain assignment?
check.a: There can be several roads between the same two cities. A later, more expensive road must not overwrite a cheaper one that was read earlier.

recap: Floyd-Warshall = three loops, `k` outside, relax `d[i][j]` through `k`.
Initialise with 0 on the diagonal and infinity elsewhere; guard every addition against infinity.
A negative value on the diagonal after the loops means a negative cycle.
Use it when n is small and you need many pair queries: pay O(n^3) once, answer each query in O(1).
Keep the minimum when the input can repeat an edge.

check_yourself.a: 400^3 = 64 million simple steps, which is fine within about a second.

check_yourself.q: When would you pick Bellman-Ford over Floyd-Warshall?
check_yourself.a: When you only need distances from one source (or n is too big for n^3) and edges can be negative.

check_yourself.q: Why use `long long` for distances in Shortest Routes II?
check_yourself.a: A path can use up to n-1 roads each costing up to 10^9, so the total can exceed the `int` limit.
